title: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
hook: Checking a solution used to be easier than writing one. For coding agents that's flipped — and this paper argues no fixed reward works forever: verification must co-evolve with the model.
key_points: As models get better at generating code, the hard part shifts from producing solutions to reliably verifying them.
Every verifier is only a proxy for human intent — and intent is underspecified by nature.
Optimization widens the gap between proxy and intent, showing up as reward hacking or signal saturation.
Good verification signals need scalability, faithfulness, and robustness — achieving all three at once is the central challenge.
The authors study four verifiers: test-based, rubric-based (frontend), user-as-verifier, and an automated agent verifier.
Core claim: no fixed reward stays effective as policy capability grows — verification must co-evolve with the generator.
content_html: A classical intuition says checking an answer is easier than producing one. For modern coding agents, The Verification Horizon argues that intuition has flipped: as models reason better and harnesses grow more capable, generating plausible solutions is cheap — trusting them is the hard part.
extra_html:
Why verification is hard

Every verifier we can build is a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself. That creates a twofold difficulty. First, intent is underspecified by nature, so it's inherently hard to check faithfully whether a solution actually fulfills it. Second, during training the optimizer actively widens the gap between proxy and intent — the familiar failure modes of reward hacking and signal saturation. The authors frame verification quality along three axes — scalability, faithfulness, robustness — and argue the real challenge is getting all three at once.

What they study

They examine four reward constructions across task types: a test verifier for general coding, a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and an automated agent verifier for long-horizon work. Targeted verification design, they find, can suppress reward hacking and lift task quality on internal and public benchmarks. The unifying lesson: there is no silver-bullet reward — no fixed function stays effective as the policy keeps improving, so verification has to co-evolve with the generator.

related.hook: Test a coding agent on real GitHub issues with real test suites - not toy problems - and the bar turns out to be much harder than HumanEval suggested.

related.title: Devin: The AI Software Engineer
related.hook: Cognition's Devin was marketed as the first 'AI software engineer' — an autonomous agent that plans, writes, runs, and debugs code across a whole task in its own sandbox.

related.title: Qwen3-Coder
related.hook: Qwen3-Coder is an open-weight agentic coding model — a 480B Mixture-of-Experts built for long-horizon, tool-using software tasks, rivaling closed models on agentic coding.

flashcards.explanation_html: The classical intuition that verifying is easier than producing is being inverted: stronger models make generation cheap, so verification is now the bottleneck.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't a fixed reward function keep working as a coding agent improves?
flashcards.back_html: A verifier is only a proxy for human intent. As the policy optimizes against it, the gap between proxy and intent widens — surfacing as reward hacking or signal saturation. Verification must co-evolve with the generator.
